impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's precedential Penumbra decision correctly held that Dynamic Drinkware's written description requirement for establishing a reference patent's priority date applies only under pre-AIA law and not under AIA § 102(d)(2).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the PTAB's finding that claims of the '409 patent were unpatentable as obvious, questioning the Board's Penumbra framework for determining whether a reference patent qualifies as prior art based on its provisional application filing date under AIA § 102. This decision could reshape how the PTAB assesses prior art dates for patents claiming provisional application priority under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit from stricter scrutiny of whether challenger references actually qualify as prior art based on provisional filing dates, potentially preserving more patents from IPR invalidation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status of reference patents that claim priority to provisional applications, increasing the cost and uncertainty of patent challenges.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial with instructions to consider two previously rejected damages models, reversed the district court's reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award, and affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability. This decision provides important guidance on permissible damages methodologies in trade secret cases under both the DTSA and state trade secret statutes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret owners benefit from the reinstated jury verdict on contract damages and the expanded consideration of damages models, strengthening remedies for misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing relationships may face broader damages exposure, as courts must consider a wider range of damages theories in trade secret cases.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee had ceased business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights, entitling the licensee to sue in its own name without joining the university. The court also held that shifting business operations to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations that would trigger automatic termination. This clarifies the rights of exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent monetization entities gain clarity that licensing agreements conveying all substantial rights allow them to sue independently, and that enforcement-focused business models do not necessarily trigger termination clauses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing challenges to exclusive licensees, and universities or patent owners may have less control over enforcement once they grant exclusive licenses with broad rights.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to communication constellation technology while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed the jury verdict on infringement and damages. The decision provides nuanced guidance on § 101 eligibility for technology-standards patents, distinguishing between claims that recite specific technical implementations and those that are more abstract.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications and standards-essential technology retain protection where claims recite specific technical implementations, and the affirmance of infringement and damages supports enforcement of technology patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement risk, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about which formulations of standards-related claims will survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment provision, or whether the dispute is purely a state-law contract matter.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a dispute about whether asserted patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the controversy to be a state-law contract interpretation issue rather than one necessarily depending on a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for post-settlement patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements gain clarity that contract interpretation disputes may be resolved in regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit, potentially benefiting those who prefer regional circuit law.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies drafting patent settlement agreements with contingent payments tied to PTO proceedings face uncertainty about which court will interpret such provisions, requiring more careful drafting to anticipate jurisdictional issues.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's statute of limitations for Court of Federal Claims suits is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities implicitly overruled the Federal Circuit's prior holding in Bright v. United States. Bank holding companies that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis due to government-sponsored enterprise investments were barred from pursuing takings and breach of contract claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies and investors pursuing claims against the federal government face a hard six-year deadline that cannot be extended by participation in a class action, significantly limiting the ability to preserve large-scale financial claims through class litigation strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a court assessing copyright infringement damages against the government must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement, and what role post-infringement evidence ('book of wisdom') plays in calculating a hypothetical negotiation royalty.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright damages rather than deferring to an existing license agreement, but vacated in part because the court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This decision provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology, particularly regarding the limits of using post-infringement evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of hypothetical negotiation as a valid damages framework that need not be constrained by existing license terms.
impacts.negativeImplications: Copyright holders face limitations on using post-infringement developments to inflate damages, and the ruling constrains the types of evidence that can be used in royalty calculations.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical method patent, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking a generic competitor from entering the market for Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The decision reinforces that courts must require bonds in patent preliminary injunctions even when equities favor the patent holder, protecting generic manufacturers from uncompensated harm if the injunction is later overturned.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction, maintaining market exclusivity during litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued market exclusion, though the bond requirement provides some financial protection. Patent holders must now post bonds even when they demonstrate strong likelihood of success, increasing the cost of obtaining injunctive relief.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's design patent infringement framework under Egyptian Goddess improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction of functional elements in design patents raises fact questions for juries.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc on design patent infringement standards, with a divided court debating whether the Egyptian Goddess framework improperly allows summary judgment based on design differences without adequate prior art analysis. The denial preserves the current framework but highlights significant judicial disagreement about how design patent infringement should be assessed, with four judges dissenting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of design patent infringement retain the ability to obtain summary judgment by demonstrating clear visual differences between designs under the existing Egyptian Goddess framework.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts may resolve infringement at summary judgment by focusing on differences rather than overall similarity, potentially weakening design patent protection.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patent claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding infringement and validity of a drug-eluting stent patent, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. This eliminates a significant damages award against a major medical device company and narrows the scope of patent protection for biodegradable polymer fiber drug delivery technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal, eliminating damages liability and establishing that the prior art anticipated the claimed drug-delivery technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face narrower protection for incremental innovations in established technology fields, as courts may more readily find anticipation by prior art.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute and exceeds the agency's delegated authority.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day regulatory filing deadline for sunset review participation is a permissible exercise of agency authority where the statute is silent on timing. The decision reinstates Commerce's procedural framework for antidumping duty sunset reviews, which affects the continuation or revocation of antidumping duty orders protecting domestic manufacturers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the preservation of Commerce's established procedural framework for sunset reviews, which helps maintain antidumping protections against unfairly priced imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face continued strict procedural requirements in sunset reviews, with a narrow 15-day window to indicate participation that could affect whether antidumping duties remain in effect.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without granting leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent case without leave to amend, the award of over $207,000 in attorney fees to Volkswagen as an exceptional case under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The decision reinforces that courts may impose significant financial consequences on patent plaintiffs and their attorneys who pursue meritless infringement claims, particularly where counsel acts in bad faith.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against frivolous patent suits benefit from robust fee-shifting and sanctions mechanisms that deter abusive patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face heightened risk of personal financial liability for pursuing weak infringement claims, particularly when filing in venues with questionable jurisdiction.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court, after dismissing a patent case for improper venue, may also dismiss on the merits under § 101 patent eligibility in the same order.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal of a patent case for both improper venue and patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, holding that the court did not err by reaching the merits even after finding venue improper. The '979 e-commerce patent was found ineligible. This decision establishes that courts may efficiently resolve both venue and eligibility challenges simultaneously.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses targeted by patent assertion entities in inconvenient venues benefit from the ability to obtain simultaneous dismissals on both venue and merits grounds, providing broader preclusive effect against future suits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that a venue dismissal will be accompanied by a merits ruling on eligibility that could have broader collateral effects on their patent portfolio.
